1 Kings — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

The history in this book describes the kingdoms of Judah and Israel.

But its special concern is the way God's kingdom was present among the people.

It is therefore sacred history.

The events it records occurred in an earlier period than the events described in ordinary histories.

This account also teaches us far more and is of greater interest than ordinary historical works.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid's declining age.1–4Adonijah aspires to the throne.5–10David makes Solomon king.11–31Solomon is anointed king, and Adonijah's usurpation stopped.32–53
David grows old (verses 1–4)

David had become weak in his old age.

He was experiencing the correction of his recent sins and the lasting effects of his earlier labors and hardships.

Adonijah tries to take the throne (verses 5–10)

Parents who indulge their children instead of correcting them often suffer afterward through those children's disobedience and impatience to possess the family inheritance.

Neither worldly wisdom, long experience nor an outwardly holy reputation can guarantee that someone ruled by selfishness will remain on a good path.

We may especially wonder how Joab and Abiathar allowed themselves to be drawn into Adonijah's rebellion.

David confirms Solomon as king (verses 11–31)

Consider Nathan's words to Bathsheba.

He offered her advice intended to save both her life and her son's.

Ministers of Christ give us similar counsel in his name.

They urge us to be diligent so that no one takes our crown (Revelation 3:11) and so that our own souls are saved.

David made a solemn declaration that he would keep his earlier decision to appoint Solomon as his successor.

As the weakness of old age increased and death approached, David remembered the many troubles from which the Lord had rescued him.

These memories increased his comfort, strengthened his hope and encouraged him to perform his remaining duty.

Solomon is anointed; Adonijah's plan collapses (verses 32–53)

The people rejoiced greatly when Solomon became king.

Every true Israelite likewise rejoices at the exaltation of the Son of David.

Conspiracies founded upon evil principles collapse quickly when personal interests shift.

How can people who do evil expect joyful news?

Adonijah had despised Solomon, but he soon feared him.

This scene helps us understand the exaltation of Jesus Christ, Son of David and Son of God, to his glorious throne despite all opposition.

His kingdom is much greater than David's, and all God's people rejoice sincerely in its advancement.

But the prosperity of Christ's kingdom brings grief and fear to its enemies.

Clinging to an altar's horns, observing outward religious forms, or claiming to be devout will not help people who refuse his authority and salvation.

If their submission is merely hypocritical, they face destruction without remedy.
classic_reading:
[1Kgs.1.1-1Kgs.1.4]
1 Kings
The history now before us accounts for the affairs of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, yet with special regard to the kingdom of God among them; for it is a sacred history. It is earlier as to time, teaches much more, and is more interesting than any common histories.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
David's declining age. | (1-4) |
Adonijah aspires to the throne. | (5-10) |
David makes Solomon king. | (11-31) |
Solomon is anointed king, and Adonijah's usurpation stopped. | (32-53) |
Verses 1-4
We have David sinking under infirmities. He was chastised for his recent sins, and felt the effects of his former toils and hardships.
[1Kgs.1.5-1Kgs.1.10]
Verses 5-10
Indulgent parents are often chastised with disobedient children, who are anxious to possess their estates. No worldly wisdom, nor experience, nor sacredness of character, can insure the continuance in any former course of those who remain under the power of self-love. But we may well wonder by what arts Joab and Abiathar could be drawn aside.
[1Kgs.1.11-1Kgs.1.31]
Verses 11-31
Observe Nathan's address to Bathsheba. Let me give thee counsel how to save thy own life, and the life of thy son. Such as this is the counsel Christ's ministers give us in his name, to give all diligence, not only that no man take our crown, [Rev.3.11] Re 3:11, but that we save our lives, even the lives of our souls. David made a solemn declaration of his firm cleaving to his former resolution, that Solomon should be his successor. Even the recollection of the distresses from which the Lord redeemed him, increased his comfort, inspired his hopes, and animated him to his duty, under the decays of nature and the approach of death.
[1Kgs.1.32-1Kgs.1.53]
Verses 32-53
The people expressed great joy and satisfaction in the elevation of Solomon. Every true Israelite rejoices in the exaltation of the Son of David. Combinations formed upon evil principles will soon be dissolved, when self-interest calls another way. How can those who do evil deeds expect to have good tidings? Adonijah had despised Solomon, but soon dreaded him. We see here, as in a glass, Jesus, the Son of David and the Son of God, exalted to the throne of glory, notwithstanding all his enemies. His kingdom is far greater than that of his father David, and therein all the true people of God cordially rejoice. The prosperity of his cause is vexation and terror to his enemies. No horns of the altar, nor forms of godliness, nor pretences to religion, can profit those who will not submit to His authority, and accept of his salvation; and if their submission be hypocritical, they shall perish without remedy.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid's dying charge to Solomon.1–4David's charge as to Joab and others.5–11Solomon reigns, Adonijah aspiring to the throne is put to death.12–25Abiathar banished, Joab put to death.26–34Shimei is put to death.35–46
David's final instruction to Solomon (verses 1–4)

David told Solomon to keep the Lord's command.

A dying father's authority deserves serious respect, but it is far below that of the living God.

The Lord had promised that the Messiah would come from David's descendants, and that promise was unconditional.

But the promise that David's family would never lack someone on Israel's throne was conditional.

The descendants must walk before God sincerely, with zeal and determination.

To do this, Solomon would need to watch over his own conduct carefully.

David's instructions about Joab and others (verses 5–11)

David's dying counsel concerning Joab and Shimei did not arise from private anger.

It was intended to preserve Solomon's throne and prevent future wrongdoing.

Joab had already committed murders, and David believed he would repeat them if doing so furthered his plans.

Although punishment had been delayed, Joab would finally be called to account.

The passage of time does not erase guilt, especially the guilt of murder.

David warned Solomon not to regard Shimei as innocent or a genuine supporter.

He believed the same malice still remained in Shimei's heart.

David's final words are recorded as spoken under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (2 Samuel 23:1–7).

In them the Lord revealed to David the offices and salvation of the coming Messiah.

All David's hope and comfort rested upon that Savior.

The passage gives convincing evidence that David died with genuine faith and hope, under the Spirit's influence.

Adonijah's request leads to his death (verses 12–25)

Solomon treated his mother Bathsheba with all the honor due to her.

But we should never ask a person to do something that person has no right to grant.

A godly person should neither make an improper request nor support an unjust cause.

In the royal customs of the time, Adonijah's request to marry Abishag clearly expressed another attempt to seize the throne.

Solomon could not be secure while Adonijah continued that ambition.

Restless, ambitious people often prepare their own destruction.

Many have lost their lives trying to seize a crown.

Abiathar loses office; Joab is executed (verses 26–34)

Solomon's words to Abiathar, and Abiathar's silence, suggest that recent conspiracies had been taking place.

Kindness shown toward God's people will be remembered favorably.

Solomon spared Abiathar's life because of his earlier service, but removed him from his offices.

The altar provided refuge in matters where the appointed sacrifice could atone.

But Joab's murders did not fall within that category.

Solomon looked to God as the Author of peace and toward eternity for peace's perfect fulfillment.

The Lord of peace himself will give us everlasting peace.

Shimei is punished (verses 35–46)

Old hostility remains within a heart that has not been changed.

We should be cautious about people who have demonstrated enmity but shown no evidence of repentance.

Worldly people can become so determined to pursue their own plans that neither solemn commitments nor danger will restrain them.

They continue even when doing so forfeits their lives and souls.

God will not bend his judgment to suit our preferences.

He sees everything we do.

We should live as though continually in his presence, because we are.

Every act, word and thought should be governed by the knowledge that a time is approaching when the smallest details of our lives will be revealed and our eternal condition will be fixed by an entirely righteous Judge.

Solomon's throne was established in peace.

It pictured the Redeemer's kingdom of peace and righteousness.

Although Christ's enemies rage, they plot in vain.

His throne stands firm, and no one can overthrow it.
classic_reading:
[1Kgs.2.1-1Kgs.2.4]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
David's dying charge to Solomon. | (1-4) |
David's charge as to Joab and others. | (5-11) |

Verses 1-4
David's charge to Solomon is, to keep the charge of the Lord. The authority of a dying father is much, but nothing to that of a living God. God promised David that the Messiah should come from his descendants, and that promise was absolute; but the promise, that there should not fail of them a man on the throne of Israel, was conditional; if he walks before God in sincerity, with zeal and resolution: in order hereunto, he must take heed to his way. ( [1Kgs.2.5-1Kgs.2.11] 1Ki 2:5-11)
[1Kgs.2.5-1Kgs.2.11]
Verses 5-11
These dying counsels concerning Joab and Shimei, did not come from personal anger, but for the security of Solomon's throne, which was the murders he had committed, but would readily repeat them to carry any purpose; though long reprieved, he shall be reckoned with at last. Time does not wear out the guilt of any sin, particularly of murder. Concerning Shimei, Hold him not guiltless; do not think him any true friend to thee, or thy government, or fit to be trusted; he has no less malice now than he had then. David's dying sentiments are recorded, as delivered under the influence of the Holy Ghost, [2Sam.23.1-2Sam.23.7] 2Sa 23:1-7. The Lord discovered to him the offices and the salvation of that glorious personage, the Messiah, whose coming he then foretold, and from whom he derived all his comforts and expectations. That passage gives a decided proof that David died under the influence of the Holy Ghost, in the exercise of faith and hope.
[1Kgs.2.12-1Kgs.2.25]
Verses 12-25
Solomon received Bathsheba with all the respect that was owing to a mother; but let none be asked for that which they ought not to grant. It ill becomes a good man to prefer a bad request, or to appear in a bad cause. According to eastern customs it was plain that Adonijah sought to be king, by his asking for Abishag as his wife, and Solomon could not be safe while he lived. Ambitious, turbulent spirits commonly prepare death for themselves. Many a head has been lost by catching at a crown.
[1Kgs.2.26-1Kgs.2.34]
Verses 26-34
Solomon's words to Abiathar, and his silence, imply that some recent conspiracies had been entered into. Those that show kindness to God's people shall have it remembered to their advantage. For this reason Solomon spares Abiathar's life, but dismisses him from his offices. In case of such sins as the blood of beasts would atone for, the altar was a refuge, but not in Joab's case. Solomon looks upward to God as the Author of peace, and forward to eternity as the perfection of it. The Lord of peace himself gives us that peace which is everlasting.
[1Kgs.2.35-1Kgs.2.46]
Verses 35-46
The old malignity remains in the unconverted heart, and a watchful eye should be kept on those who, like Shimei, have manifested their enmity, but have given no evidence of repentance. No engagements or dangers will restrain worldly men; they go on, though they forfeit their lives and souls. Let us remember, God will not accommodate his judgment to us. His eye is over us; and let us strive to walk as in his presence. Let our every act, word, and thought, be governed by this great truth, that the hour is quickly coming when the smallest circumstances of our lives shall be brought to light, and our eternal state be fixed by a righteous and unerring God. Thus Solomon's throne was established in peace, as the type of the Redeemer's kingdom of peace and righteousness. And it is a comfort, in reference to the enmity of the church's enemies, that, how much soever they rage, it is a vain thing they imagine. Christ's throne is established, and they cannot shake it.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesSolomon's marriage.1–4His vision, His prayer for wisdom.5–15The judgment of Solomon.16–28
Solomon loves the Lord (verses 1–4)

Someone who loves the Lord should, for his sake, seek a spouse among the Lord's own people.

Solomon was wise, wealthy and powerful.

Yet his brightest commendation was one shared by every genuine believer, even the poorest: he loved the Lord.

Where God gives much, he rightly expects much in return.

Those who genuinely love him and his worship will not resent the cost of serving him.

We should never regard what we spend in God's service as wasted.

Solomon asks for wisdom (verses 5–15)

Solomon's dream was no ordinary dream.

Although his bodily powers were asleep, God strengthened his mind and soul so that he could receive a divine vision and make a fitting choice.

The Lord likewise puts us on the way toward true happiness by assuring us that he will provide what we genuinely need and ask for.

Solomon's decision, made while his ordinary reasoning faculties were least active, showed that the choice arose from God's grace.

He felt humbly how little wisdom and strength he possessed.

He pleaded that he was like a small child.

The wiser and more thoughtful people become, the more clearly they recognize their weakness and the more cautious they become about trusting their own judgment.

Solomon asked God for wisdom.

We must do the same (James 1:5), so that we can fulfill our own calling and respond well to the many circumstances we face.

The Lord accepts people who prize spiritual blessings above earthly advantages.

Solomon's prayer was effective—and God gave him more than he asked.

He received wisdom greater than that of any other ruler, together with wealth and honor.

If we secure wisdom and grace, they may bring outward benefits, or they will sweeten the lack of those benefits.

To receive spiritual blessings, we must seek them earnestly in prayer.

Concerning earthly benefits, we must entrust ourselves to God's decision.

Solomon received wisdom because he asked for it, and wealth because he did not ask for it.

Solomon identifies the true mother (verses 16–28)

This judgment demonstrates Solomon's God-given wisdom.

The situation was difficult.

To discover which woman was the child's mother, he could not test which woman the child loved most.

He therefore tested which woman loved the child most.

When a child appeared to be in danger, the true mother's love became clear.

Parents should show love to their children chiefly by caring for their souls, seeking to rescue them like brands from a fire.

Solomon's wisdom in this and other judgments made him greatly respected throughout Israel.

Such wisdom did him more good than weapons of war.

Through it he became both feared and loved.

Verses 1-4
He that loved the Lord, should, for his sake, have fixed his love upon one of the Lord's people. Solomon was a wise man, a rich man, a great man; yet the brightest praise of him, is that which is the character of all the saints, even the poorest, "He loved the Lord." Where God sows plentifully, he expects to reap accordingly; and those that truly love God and his worship, will not grudge the expenses of their religion. We must never think that wasted which is laid out in the service of God.
[1Kgs.3.5-1Kgs.3.15]
Verses 5-15
Solomon's dream was not a common one. While his bodily powers were locked up in sleep, the powers of his soul were strengthened; he was enabled to receive the Divine vision, and to make a suitable choice. God, in like manner, puts us in the ready way to be happy, by assuring us we shall have what we need, and pray for. Solomon's making such a choice when asleep, and the powers of reason least active, showed it came from the grace of God. Having a humble sense of his own wants and weakness, he pleads, Lord, I am but a little child. The more wise and considerate men are, the better acquainted they are with their own weakness, and the more jealous of themselves. Solomon begs of God to give him wisdom. We must pray for it, [Jas.1.5] Jas 1:5, that it may help us in our particular calling, and the various occasions we have. Those are accepted of God, who prefer spiritual blessings to earthly good. It was a prevailing prayer, and prevailed for more than he asked. God gave him wisdom, such as no other prince was ever blessed with; and also gave him riches and honour. If we make sure of wisdom and grace, these will bring outward prosperity with them, or sweeten the want of it. The way to get spiritual blessings, is to wrestle with God in prayer for them. The way to get earthly blessings, is to refer ourselves to God concerning them. Solomon has wisdom given him, because he did ask it, and wealth, because he did not.
[1Kgs.3.16-1Kgs.3.28]
Verses 16-28
An instance of Solomon's wisdom is given. Notice the difficulty of the case. To find out the true mother, he could not try which the child loved best, and therefore tried which loved the child best: the mother's sincerity will be tried, when the child is in danger. Let parents show their love to their children, especially by taking care of their souls, and snatching them as brands out of the burning. By this and other instances of the wisdom with which God endued him, Solomon had great reputation among his people. This was better to him than weapons of war; for this he was both feared and loved.

Solomon appoints his officials (verses 1–19)

Solomon's wisdom surely showed itself in his choice of leading officials.

Several of them had also served during David's reign.

Solomon arranged the kingdom's contributions so that no single district was exhausted by the responsibility of supplying the royal household.

Every region gave its proper share.

Solomon's kingdom enjoys peace (verses 20–28)

Israel's royal crown never shone more brightly than it did when Solomon wore it.

Peace surrounded his kingdom.

In this it pictured the kingdom of the Messiah, who would receive the nations as his inheritance and to whom princes would come in worship.

The spiritual peace, joy and holy security enjoyed by all faithful subjects of the Lord Jesus were pictured by Israel's earthly happiness.

But God's kingdom is not food and drink.

It consists of something infinitely better: righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

The enormous amount of food prepared for Solomon's household shows the crowds who served and visited him.

Christ is greater than Solomon.

He feeds all his people, not with perishable bread, but with the food that endures to eternal life.

Solomon's God-given wisdom (verses 29–34)

Solomon's wisdom brought him more honor than his wealth.

He possessed what Scripture calls largeness of heart, meaning extraordinary mental capacity.

He received both wisdom and the ability to communicate it effectively.

Those with great gifts should have equally generous hearts, using their abilities for the benefit of others.

How much wisdom and knowledge is wasted when people do not share what they possess!

Yet the holy Scriptures contain every kind of knowledge necessary for salvation.

People came from faraway places because they valued knowledge more highly than their neighbors.

Solomon pictured Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

Those riches are hidden for us: Christ has been made our wisdom by God.

His fame will spread throughout the earth.

People of every nation will come to him, learn from him, take his gentle yoke upon themselves and find rest for their souls.

Solomon makes an agreement with Hiram (verses 1–9)

Solomon intended to build the Lord's temple.

At this time Israel had no enemy, no Satan—that is how Henry explains the word.

There was no instrument of Satan hindering Solomon's plans or drawing him away from his purpose.

Satan constantly tries to obstruct work done for God's house.

When no active obstacle stands before us, we should be especially ready to do what is good.

God's promises should strengthen and quicken our efforts.

Every worldly talent, advantage and practical skill should be used in the interests of Christ's kingdom.

Tyre supplied Israel with craftsmen, while Israel supplied Tyre with grain (Ezekiel 27:17).

In the wisdom of divine Providence, one nation needs and benefits another.

This mutual dependence gives people opportunities to glorify God.

Workers prepare the temple materials (verses 10–18)

The temple was largely built through the wealth and labor of Gentiles.

This pictured the future calling of the Gentile peoples into God's church.

Solomon commanded that expensive stones be prepared for the foundation.

Jesus Christ is the chosen and precious Foundation Stone.

We should make sure the foundation of our faith is secure.

The part of our religious lives that people cannot see deserves our greatest care and effort.

Blessed are those who become living stones, joined together into a spiritual house in which God dwells through his Spirit.

Who among us will help build the Lord's house?

Here is Solomon's design to build a temple. There is no adversary, no Satan, so the word is; no instrument of Satan to oppose it, or to divert from it. Satan does all he can, to hinder temple work. Solomon builds the temple (verses 1–10)

The building was called the house of the Lord because God himself directed its form and construction.

It was to be devoted to his service.

This made it beautiful with the beauty of holiness, a beauty greater than every outward ornament.

It was a temple for the God of peace.

Therefore no iron tool was to be heard during its construction.

Quietness and silence are fitting for religious devotion and help us carry it out.

God's work should be performed carefully, but with little noise.

Shouting, disorder and violence tend to obstruct rather than advance his work.

So too God's kingdom grows silently within the human heart.

Henry attaches the reference Mark 5:27 to this image.

God's promise and warning to Solomon (verses 11–14)

Whenever people work for God, his eye is upon them.

But God warned Solomon plainly that the great responsibility and expense of building the temple could not excuse disobedience to divine law.

Nor would building such a house protect him from judgment if he turned away from the Lord's commands.

The spiritual meanings of the temple (verses 15–38)

Henry identifies four realities pictured by this temple.

First, Christ himself is the true Temple.

In him all the fullness of deity dwells.

All God's spiritual Israel meet in him.

Through him we approach God with confidence.

Second, each believer is a living temple.

The Spirit of God dwells within the believer (1 Corinthians 3:16).

This living sanctuary is built upon Christ as its foundation and will become perfect at the appointed time.

Third, the gospel church is God's spiritual Temple.

It grows into a holy temple in the Lord, enriched and beautified by the Spirit's gifts and graces.

It stands firmly upon the Rock.

Fourth, heaven is the eternal Temple.

There God's people will remain forever.

Everyone who will become part of that heavenly building must be prepared and fitted for it during the present life.

Let sinners come to Jesus, the living Foundation, so that they may be built upon him, made part of his spiritual house and devoted in body and soul to God's glory.

Solomon builds his other houses (verses 1–12)

All Solomon's buildings were beautiful, but they were also intended for practical use.

Solomon began with the temple.

He built for God before building his other houses.

The surest foundations of lasting prosperity are laid in early devotion to the Lord.

Solomon spent thirteen years building his palace but a little more than seven years building the temple.

That did not mean he cared less about the quality of his own house.

He simply gave greater urgency and effort to the Lord's work than to his own comfort.

We should likewise value God's honor above our ease and satisfaction.

Furnishings for the temple (verses 13–47)

The two bronze pillars at the temple entrance may, Henry says, have taught worshipers to depend on God alone for stability and strength in every act of worship.

Jachin can be understood as, “God will establish this wandering heart.”

It is good for the heart to be established by grace.

Boaz points to strength found in God, who works within us both to will and to act.

Spiritual strength and stability are received at the door of God's temple as we wait upon his appointed means of grace.

Spiritual priests and spiritual sacrifices must be washed in the cleansing basin of Christ's blood and regeneration.

We must wash frequently because we become defiled by sin every day.

The Lord has provided everything necessary for cleansing.

If we finally remain among the unclean, we have only ourselves to blame for rejecting what he provided.

Let us praise God for the fountain opened by Christ's sacrifice for sin and impurity.

The vessels of gold (verses 48–51)

Christ is now both the Temple and its Builder.

He is the Altar and the Sacrifice.

He is the Light of our souls and the Bread of Life.

He can meet every need of those who have come or will come to him.

No outward image can adequately represent his worth.

Words cannot express it, and the human mind cannot fully imagine his love.

Come to him.

Let his blood wash away your sins, and seek the cleansing grace of his Spirit.

Through his intercession, remain in fellowship with the Father.

Give yourself and everything you possess to his service.

Strengthened by him, you will become accepted, useful and happy.

The ark is placed in the temple (verses 1–11)

Bringing the ark into the temple completed the work.

The people did so with great solemnity.

The ark was placed inside the Most Holy Place, where Israel expected God to speak from his mercy seat.

The poles were drawn out so that they pointed toward the mercy seat and guided the high priest when he entered once a year to sprinkle blood.

They were still useful, even though they were no longer needed for carrying the ark.

God's glory appeared in a cloud.

Henry sees two images in this darkness.

First, the earlier religious order was comparatively dark when set beside the light of the gospel, through which believers behold the Lord's glory more openly.

Second, our present lives are comparatively dark when set beside heaven, where God's glory will be fully revealed and seeing him will make his people happy.

Solomon encourages the priests (verses 12–21)

The priests were astonished by the dark cloud.

Solomon encouraged them.

When God's providence seems dark, we should hurry toward the hope given in the gospel.

The best comfort comes from remembering God's word and considering his works in its light.

Whenever we accomplish something good, we should see it as God fulfilling his promise to us, not merely us fulfilling promises we made to him.

Solomon prays to God (verses 22–53)

Solomon's prayer is a model for ours.

He gave glory to God before seeking further blessings.

New experiences of God's faithfulness should lead to fuller praise.

We should appeal to his promises, depending upon them in our requests.

People who desire new mercies should remain thankful for those already received.

God's promises should guide what we desire and form the ground of what we hope for in prayer.

The sacrifices, incense and ministry of the temple pictured Christ's priestly office, offering and intercession.

That is why people were to keep the temple in mind.

One word expresses all Solomon sought for Israel: “forgive.”

Every misery ultimately springs from sin.

Forgiveness therefore opens the way for the removal of evil and reception of good.

Without pardon, even an outward deliverance cannot become a true blessing.

Solomon also asked God to teach the people through his word and through his discipline, making their suffering spiritually useful.

Each person must recognize the plague of his own heart.

This includes the painful burden of guilt and the sinful desires still living within us.

Every true believer should learn to recognize these spiritual diseases, watch against their return and put them to death.

Awareness of inward sin drives us to prayer.

Solomon ultimately asked the Lord to hear his praying people.

Under the gospel, no special building or physical direction adds anything to a prayer.

Christ is the reality to which the temple pointed.

Whatever we ask in his name according to God's promise may be granted.

Through Christ, God's people are established and sanctified, the wanderer restored, the foreigner welcomed, mourners comforted and God's name glorified.

Sin causes our troubles; repentance and forgiveness lead toward human happiness.

Solomon blesses and exhorts Israel (verses 54–61)

Solomon's farewell words were especially likely to remain with the people.

The blessings he requested are now obtained through Christ's intercession, of which his prayer was a type.

We receive sufficient, suitable and timely grace whenever we truly need it.

No human heart is naturally willing to obey the gospel call to repentance, faith and a renewed life.

Yet Solomon called the people to walk wholeheartedly in God's commands.

That is the way Scripture teaches us.

We must obey the law and the gospel's summons.

Because we know how sinful and weak we are, we pray for divine help, through which Christ enables us to serve God.

Solomon celebrates with offerings (verses 62–66)

Solomon made many sacrifices.

He apparently observed the Feast of Tabernacles after the temple dedication.

Let us likewise return home rejoicing after worship, thankful for the Lord's goodness.

In this excellent prayer, Solomon does as we should do in every prayer; he gives glory to God. Fresh experiences of the truth of God's promises call for larger praises. He sues for grace and favour from God. The experiences we have of God's performing his promises, should encourage us to depend upon them, and to plead them with him; and those who expect further mercies, must be thankful for former mercies. God's promises must be the guide of our desires, and the ground of our hopes and expectations in prayer. The sacrifices, the incense, and the whole service of the temple, were all typical of the Redeemer's offices, oblation, and intercession. The temple, therefore, was continually to be remembered. Under one word, "forgive," Solomon expressed all that he could ask in behalf of his people. For, as all misery springs from sin, forgiveness of sin prepares the way for the removal of every evil, and the receiving of every good. Without it, no deliverance can prove a blessing. In addition to the teaching of the word of God, Solomon entreated the Lord himself to teach the people to profit by all, even by their chastisements. God answers Solomon's prayer (verses 1–9)

After Solomon completed and dedicated the temple, the Lord warned him against pride and called him to reverent fear.

Even after all the service we can offer, our standing before God remains the same.

Nothing we do can purchase permission to sin.

A genuine believer would never desire such permission.

The believer would rather be corrected by God than continue comfortably and prosperously in wrongdoing.

Solomon and Hiram exchange gifts (verses 10–14)

Solomon gave twenty cities to Hiram.

Hiram was displeased with them.

If Solomon wanted to please him, it would be better to cooperate with him in trade, as the two kings eventually did.

See how God's providence suits different parts of the earth to people's varied needs and dispositions.

He also suits people to the lands where they live.

Through this arrangement, human beings depend upon one another and work together for their common benefit.

Solomon's prosperity and trade (verses 15–28)

This passage further describes Solomon's greatness.

He began in the right order.

He built God's house first, and only after finishing it did he undertake his own palace.

Then the Lord blessed his other building projects with success.

Let devotion come first, profit afterward, and pleasure last.

When we make real sacrifices for God's glory and for other people's good, the work may also bring benefit to us.

Canaan, the holy land and glory of all lands, had no gold of its own.

This reminds us that the most valuable production is often what sustains human life—our own lives and our neighbors'—rather than what brings luxury.

Canaan produced those necessary goods.

Solomon gained much wealth through commerce.

Yet he recommended a better trade, one available even to the poorest people.

Wisdom is better than silver, and its profit is greater than fine gold (Proverbs 3:14).

The queen of Sheba visits Solomon (verses 1–13)

The queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon's wisdom so that she might increase her own understanding.

Our Savior refers to her search for knowledge of God through Solomon in order to rebuke those who fail to seek God through Jesus Christ himself.

We, too, can find our way through difficulties by waiting upon God in prayer, diligently searching the Scriptures, seeking advice from wise and experienced Christians, and putting what we learn into practice.

Solomon's wisdom impressed the queen more deeply than his riches, power and magnificence.

The excellence of heavenly things, and of Christians whose conduct agrees with their faith, is greater than any report about them can adequately express.

In the queen's experience the truth exceeded the reports.

All who, by grace, enjoy fellowship with God will likewise discover that not even half the pleasure and benefit of walking in wisdom was told them beforehand.

How much more will the glorified saints say, when they enter heaven, that not even a thousandth part of its happiness had been described to them (1 Corinthians 2:9)!

The queen called those who continually attended Solomon happy.

We have still greater reason to call the servants of Christ blessed: those who dwell in his house will continue praising him.

She brought Solomon a generous gift.

Christ does not need anything we give him, but he calls us to give as an expression of gratitude.

A believer who has enjoyed fellowship with Jesus will return to ordinary responsibilities ready to fulfill them with better motives, while looking forward to the day when being absent from the body will mean being present with the Lord.

Solomon's riches (verses 14–29)

Solomon's wealth increased until silver was scarcely valued.

This is the nature of worldly riches: when they become plentiful, people tend to value them less.

How much more should the enjoyment of spiritual wealth diminish our attachment to earthly possessions!

If abundant gold makes silver seem insignificant, should not wisdom, grace and foretastes of heaven—which are worth far more than gold—make gold itself seem small to us?

Solomon's greatness fulfilled God's promise.

Let that encourage us to seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness.

Yet Solomon was also the man who, after experiencing every kind of earthly pleasure, wrote a book declaring that worldly things are vanity, accompanied by vexation of spirit, and that setting our hearts on them is foolish.

He recommended sincere godliness as bringing far greater happiness than all the riches and power he possessed.

Through God's grace, that true happiness is available to us.

The queen of Sheba came to Solomon to hear his wisdom, thereby to improve her own. By waiting and prayer, by diligently searching the Scriptures, by consulting wise and experienced Christians, and by practising what we have learned, we shall be delivered from difficulties. There is a spiritual excellence in heavenly things, and in consistent Christians, to which no reports can do justice. Here the truth exceeded; and all who, through grace, are brought to commune with God, will say the one half was not told them of the pleasures and the advantages of wisdom's ways. Glorified saints, much more, will say of heaven, that the thousandth part was not told them, [1Cor.2.9] 1Co 2:9. She pronounced them happy that constantly attended Solomon. With much more reason may we say of Christ's servants, Blessed are they that dwell in his house; they will be still praising him. She made a noble present to Solomon. What we present to Christ, he needs not, but will have us do so to express our gratitude. The believer who has been with Jesus, will return to his station, discharge his duties with readiness, and from better motives; looking forward to the day when, being absent from the body, he shall be present with the Lord.
[1Kgs.10.14-1Kgs.10.29]
Verses 14-29
Solomon increased his wealth. Silver was nothing accounted of. Such is the nature of worldly wealth, plenty of it makes it the less valuable; much more should the enjoyment of spiritual riches lessen our esteem of all earthly possessions. If gold in abundance makes silver to be despised, shall not wisdom, and grace, and the foretastes of heaven, which are far better than gold, make gold to be lightly esteemed? See in Solomon's greatness the performance of God's promise, and let it encourage us to seek first the righteousness of God's kingdom. This was he, who, having tasted all earthly enjoyments, wrote a book, to show the vanity of all worldly things, the vexation of spirit that attends them, and the folly of setting our hearts upon them: and to recommend serious godliness, as that which will do unspeakably more to make us happy, that all the wealth and power he was master of; and, through the grace of God, it is within our reach.
